claim: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) are concentrated in small nanodomains around 80 nm in size.
source: AMPARs were initially thought to be homogeneously distributed throughout the PSD, but recent work based on super-resolution optical imaging (SRI) and electron microscopy has demonstrated that AMPARs are concentrated in small nanodomains around 80 nm in size, and containing 20 receptors on average (Fukata et al., 2013; MacGillavry et al., 2013; Masugi-Tokita et al., 2007; Nair et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Fukata et al., 2013; MacGillavry et al., 2013; Masugi-Tokita et al., 2007; Nair et al., 2013) that used super-resolution optical imaging and electron microscopy.

claim: AMPAR nanodomains contain 20 receptors on average.
source: AMPARs were initially thought to be homogeneously distributed throughout the PSD, but recent work based on super-resolution optical imaging (SRI) and electron microscopy has demonstrated that AMPARs are concentrated in small nanodomains around 80 nm in size, and containing 20 receptors on average (Fukata et al., 2013; MacGillavry et al., 2013; Masugi-Tokita et al., 2007; Nair et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Fukata et al., 2013; MacGillavry et al., 2013; Masugi-Tokita et al., 2007; Nair et al., 2013).

claim: The glutamate content of a single presynaptic vesicle is not sufficient to activate the entire pool of AMPARs inside the PSD.
source: Indeed, previous studies showed that the glutamate content of a single presynaptic vesicle is not sufficient to activate the entire pool of AMPARs inside the PSD (Liu et al., 1999; Raghavachari and Lisman, 2004), suggesting that synaptic currents might be stronger if AMPARs were concentrated in front of pre-synaptic release sites rather than dispersed throughout the PSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Liu et al., 1999; Raghavachari and Lisman, 2004).

claim: Mathematical models predict that when AMPARs are clustered in front of glutamate release sites, both the amplitude and the reliability of synaptic responses are improved.
source: Moreover, mathematical models predict that when AMPARs are clustered in front of glutamate release sites, both the amplitude and the reliability of synaptic responses are improved (Franks et al., 2002, Franks et al., 2003; Rusakov, 2001; Rusakov and Kullmann, 1998; Tarusawa et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple mathematical modeling studies (Franks et al., 2002, Franks et al., 2003; Rusakov, 2001; Rusakov and Kullmann, 1998; Tarusawa et al., 2009).

claim: When AMPAR clusters are not aligned with release sites, synaptic currents are predicted to be weaker and highly variable.
source: In contrast, when AMPAR clusters are not aligned with release sites, synaptic currents are predicted to be weaker and highly variable (Tarusawa et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a modeling study (Tarusawa et al., 2009).

claim: The pre-synaptic active zone protein RIM is concentrated in small domains.
source: A recent study indicated however that the pre-synaptic active zone protein RIM is concentrated in small domains (Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Tang et al., 2016).

claim: Active glutamate release sites are co-localized with RIM and aligned with AMPAR nanodomains.
source: Furthermore, this study showed that active glutamate release sites are co-localized with RIM and aligned with AMPAR nanodomains.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a study mentioned in the previous sentence (Tang et al., 2016).

claim: Trans-synaptic 'nanocolumn' organization is regulated by long-term synaptic plasticity.
source: This trans-synaptic 'nanocolumn' organization is regulated by long-term synaptic plasticity, highlighting its importance for the control of synaptic transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by implicit reference to the Tang et al., 2016 study discussed in the preceding sentences.

claim: The neurexin-neuroligin complex forms a trans-synaptic bridge.
source: It has been abundantly described that the adhesion complex neurexin-neuroligin forms a trans-synaptic bridge (Südhof, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Südhof, 2008.

claim: Pre-synaptic neurexin is implicated in active zone formation.
source: Pre-synaptic neurexin is implicated in active zone formation (Missler et al., 2003), while post-synaptic neuroligin-1 (NLG1) recruits PSD-95, NMDA receptors and AMPARs to partly structure the PSD (Budreck et al., 2013; Graf et al., 2004; Heine et al., 2008; Mondin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Missler et al., 2003.

claim: Post-synaptic neuroligin-1 (NLG1) recruits PSD-95, NMDA receptors and AMPARs to partly structure the PSD.
source: Pre-synaptic neurexin is implicated in active zone formation (Missler et al., 2003), while post-synaptic neuroligin-1 (NLG1) recruits PSD-95, NMDA receptors and AMPARs to partly structure the PSD (Budreck et al., 2013; Graf et al., 2004; Heine et al., 2008; Mondin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Budreck et al., 2013; Graf et al., 2004; Heine et al., 2008; Mondin et al., 2011).

claim: A C-terminally truncated NLG1 mutant (NLG1-ΔCter) prevents PSD-95 recruitment at newly formed synapses.
source: In particular, a C-terminally truncated NLG1 mutant, unable to bind PDZ domain containing PSD proteins (NLG1-ΔCter), was previously shown to prevent PSD-95 recruitment at newly formed synapses, and reduce AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission (Chih et al., 2005; Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chih et al., 2005; Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter reduces AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
source: In particular, a C-terminally truncated NLG1 mutant, unable to bind PDZ domain containing PSD proteins (NLG1-ΔCter), was previously shown to prevent PSD-95 recruitment at newly formed synapses, and reduce AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission (Chih et al., 2005; Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chih et al., 2005; Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005).

claim: Expression of NLG1 increases spine density.
source: As previously described (Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005), expression of both truncated and full length NLG1 (Figure 1A and B) increases spine density, revealing the synaptogenic role of NLG1 (n = 10; 12; 9 respectively; ANOVA p=0.0004).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B (ANOVA p=0.0004) and citations to previous studies (Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005).

claim: Expression of NLG1-ΔCter increases spine density.
source: As previously described (Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005), expression of both truncated and full length NLG1 (Figure 1A and B) increases spine density, revealing the synaptogenic role of NLG1 (n = 10; 12; 9 respectively; ANOVA p=0.0004).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B (ANOVA p=0.0004) and citations to previous studies (Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005).

claim: In control neurons expressing GFP alone, between 1 to 2 AMPAR nanodomains per synapse are typically detected.
source: In control neurons expressing GFP alone, we typically detected between 1 to 2 AMPAR nanodomains per synapse, with an average size of 90 ± 3 nm (Figure 1D and E), as reported previously (Nair et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E and a citation to a previous study (Nair et al., 2013).

claim: AMPAR nanodomains in control neurons have an average size of 90 ± 3 nm.
source: In control neurons expressing GFP alone, we typically detected between 1 to 2 AMPAR nanodomains per synapse, with an average size of 90 ± 3 nm (Figure 1D and E), as reported previously (Nair et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E and a citation to a previous study (Nair et al., 2013).

claim: NLG1 overexpression increased the surface density of AMPAR nanodomains.
source: NLG1 overexpression increased the surface density of AMPAR nanodomains (Figure 1C), in agreement with the previous finding that NLG1 potentiates the formation of excitatory synapses (Chih et al., 2005; Ko et al., 2009; Levinson et al., 2005; Mondin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citations to previous studies (Chih et al., 2005; Ko et al., 2009; Levinson et al., 2005; Mondin et al., 2011).

claim: NLG1 overexpression led to a re-organization of AMPAR nanodomains by increasing both their size and AMPAR content.
source: Furthermore, NLG1 overexpression led to a re-organization of AMPAR nanodomains by increasing both their size and AMPAR content (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Expression of NLG1-ΔCter for 3 days did not affect AMPAR nano-organization compared to the GFP control.
source: Surprisingly, expression of NLG1-ΔCter for 3 days did not affect AMPAR nano-organization compared to the GFP control (Figure 1C–E, ANOVA post-test: p=0.72; 0.82 and 0.33 for figure C; D and E respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E with statistical analysis (ANOVA post-test: p=0.72; 0.82 and 0.33).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter expression does not affect the total amount of AMPARs per synapse.
source: This analysis confirmed that NLG1-ΔCter expression does not affect the total amount of AMPARs per synapse, nor their organization in nanodomains.
evidence: The claim is supported by Tessellation analysis of d-STORM images described in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NLG1-ΔCter expression does not affect AMPAR organization in nanodomains.
source: This analysis confirmed that NLG1-ΔCter expression does not affect the total amount of AMPARs per synapse, nor their organization in nanodomains.
evidence: The claim is supported by Tessellation analysis of d-STORM images described in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: AMPARs exhibit two diffusion profiles: the immobile fraction represents mostly AMPARs trapped by PSD scaffolding proteins in nanodomains, whereas the mobile fraction represents individual freely moving AMPARs.
source: We previously showed that AMPARs exhibit two diffusion profiles: the immobile fraction represents mostly AMPARs trapped by PSD scaffolding proteins in nanodomains, whereas the mobile fraction represents individual freely moving AMPARs (Nair et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Nair et al., 2013).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter does not affect the distribution of diffusion coefficients of AMPARs.
source: Both the distribution of diffusion coefficients and the mobile fraction (i.e. proportion of AMPARs with diffusion coefficients above 0.01 µm²/s) were not significantly affected by NLG1-ΔCter, as compared to GFP-expressing neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, n = 16 Ctrl and 21 NLG1-ΔCter, 2 sample t-test p=0.36), in agreement with previous findings using Quantum dots (Mondin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 (n = 16 Ctrl and 21 NLG1-ΔCter, 2 sample t-test p=0.36) and a citation to a previous study (Mondin et al., 2011).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter does not affect the mobile fraction of AMPARs.
source: Both the distribution of diffusion coefficients and the mobile fraction (i.e. proportion of AMPARs with diffusion coefficients above 0.01 µm²/s) were not significantly affected by NLG1-ΔCter, as compared to GFP-expressing neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, n = 16 Ctrl and 21 NLG1-ΔCter, 2 sample t-test p=0.36), in agreement with previous findings using Quantum dots (Mondin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 (n = 16 Ctrl and 21 NLG1-ΔCter, 2 sample t-test p=0.36) and a citation to a previous study (Mondin et al., 2011).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter does not affect the equilibrium between diffusive and trapped AMPARs.
source: Thus, NLG1-ΔCter does not affect the equilibrium between diffusive and trapped AMPARs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on AMPAR diffusion and mobile fraction presented in the preceding sentences.

claim: The majority of synaptic NLG1 spots overlap with AMPAR nanodomains.
source: Qualitatively, we observed that the majority of synaptic NLG1 spots (green) overlapped with AMPAR nanodomains (purple).
evidence: The claim is based on qualitative observation of dual-color d-STORM images described in the text.

claim: NLG1 does not form large domains inside synapses, but rather several small clusters.
source: The similar area distribution between single fluorescence emitters and NLG1 clusters (Figure 2C) reveals that NLG1 does not form large domains inside synapses, but rather several small clusters, confirming previous findings with an alternative labelling strategy (Chamma et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to a previous study (Chamma et al., 2016).

claim: The bivariate nearest neighbor distance distribution between NLG1 and AMPAR nanodomains was significantly smaller than that expected from an independent distribution.
source: The centroid to centroid bivariate nearest neighbor distance distribution between NLG1 and AMPAR nanodomains was significantly smaller than that expected from an independent distribution (Figure 2D; green line, n = 512 pairs of co-localized objects), indicating a functional proximity between NLG1 and GluA2 clusters at the nanoscale.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D (n = 512 pairs of co-localized objects).

claim: Only 20% of NLG1 clusters did not co-localize, even partially, with a GluA2 nanodomain.
source: Only 20% of NLG1 clusters did not co-localize, even partially, with a GluA2 nanodomain, while 25% of NLG1 clusters co-localized to more than 80% with AMPAR nanodomains.
evidence: The claim is supported by Manders' coefficient analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 2E (n = 512 pairs of objects).

claim: 25% of NLG1 clusters co-localized to more than 80% with AMPAR nanodomains.
source: Only 20% of NLG1 clusters did not co-localize, even partially, with a GluA2 nanodomain, while 25% of NLG1 clusters co-localized to more than 80% with AMPAR nanodomains.
evidence: The claim is supported by Manders' coefficient analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 2E (n = 512 pairs of objects).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter is organized in small clusters with an average size of 0.0042 ± 0.0018 µm2.
source: As NLG1, NLG1-ΔCter was organized in small clusters (Figure 2C, red line) with an average size of 0.0042 ± 0.0018 µm2, whereas AMPARs were distributed as both small and large objects.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Centroid to centroid bivariate nearest neighbor distance between all NLG1-ΔCter object and GluA2 clusters overlapped with a random distribution for the first 250 nm corresponding to the PSD size.
source: Centroid to centroid bivariate nearest neighbor distance between all NLG1-ΔCter object and GluA2 clusters overlapped with a random distribution, at least for the first 250 nm corresponding to the PSD size (Figure 2F, red line).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is no preferential association of NLG1-ΔCter clusters with AMPAR nanodomains.
source: This led us to the conclusion that there is no preferential association of NLG1-ΔCter clusters with AMPAR nanodomains.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the bivariate nearest neighbor distance analysis described in the preceding sentence.

claim: Only 38% of NLG1-ΔCter co-localized at least partially with AMPARs, compared with 80% for NLG1.
source: Only 38% of NLG1-ΔCter co-localized at least partially with AMPARs, compared with 80% for NLG1, revealing that the NLG1 C-terminal truncation significantly decreases the association between NLG1 and AMPAR nanodomains (comparison with NLG1: 2 sample t-test p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by Manders' coefficient analysis shown in Figure 2G with statistical comparison (2 sample t-test p<0.0001).

claim: The NLG1 C-terminal truncation significantly decreases the association between NLG1 and AMPAR nanodomains.
source: Only 38% of NLG1-ΔCter co-localized at least partially with AMPARs, compared with 80% for NLG1, revealing that the NLG1 C-terminal truncation significantly decreases the association between NLG1 and AMPAR nanodomains (comparison with NLG1: 2 sample t-test p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by Manders' coefficient analysis with statistical comparison (2 sample t-test p<0.0001).

claim: The bivariate nearest neighbor distances between RIM and AMPAR clusters was not affected by NLG1 expression.
source: The bivariate nearest neighbor distances between RIM and AMPAR clusters was not affected by NLG1 expression, but was significantly larger when NLG1-ΔCter was expressed (Figure 3B, Anova p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis (Anova p<0.001).

claim: The bivariate nearest neighbor distances between RIM and AMPAR clusters was significantly larger when NLG1-ΔCter was expressed.
source: The bivariate nearest neighbor distances between RIM and AMPAR clusters was not affected by NLG1 expression, but was significantly larger when NLG1-ΔCter was expressed (Figure 3B, Anova p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis (Anova p<0.001).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter expression decreased the RIM-AMPAR apposition.
source: The distribution of Manders' coefficients confirmed that NLG1-ΔCter expression decreased the RIM-AMPAR apposition (Figure 3C, Anova p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis (Anova p<0.001).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter expression causes a physical misalignment between the presynaptic marker RIM and the postsynaptic AMPAR clusters.
source: These results demonstrate a physical misalignment between the presynaptic marker RIM and the postsynaptic AMPAR clusters upon NLG1-ΔCter expression, while NLG1 expression did not display a similar effect.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on RIM-AMPAR co-localization presented in the preceding sentences and shown in Figure 3.

claim: NLG1-ΔCter expression for 3 days reduced the amplitude of AMPAR mEPSCs by 24% as compared to GFP expressing controls.
source: NLG1-ΔCter expression for 3 days reduced the amplitude of AMPAR mEPSCs by 24% as compared to GFP expressing controls (Figure 4C, average ± SEM: 11.63 ± 0.63 for GFP, 8.956 ± 0.40 for NLG1-ΔCter, 13.05 ± 0.92 for NLG1; ANOVA p=0.0002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C with statistical analysis (ANOVA p=0.0002).

claim: NLG1 expression did not affect the miniature EPSC amplitude.
source: In contrast, NLG1 expression did not affect the miniature EPSC amplitude, even if as expected by the higher synapse number observed in Figure 1A, there was a significant increase in miniature frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NLG1 expression caused a significant increase in miniature frequency.
source: In contrast, NLG1 expression did not affect the miniature EPSC amplitude, even if as expected by the higher synapse number observed in Figure 1A, there was a significant increase in miniature frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neurons overexpressing NLG1 exhibited a ~4 fold increase in AMPAR-mediated EPSC amplitude (456.1% ± 80.0) compared to paired non-electroporated controls.
source: In the presence of 2 mM extracellular calcium, we observed a ~4 fold increase in AMPAR-mediated EPSC amplitude (456.1% ± 80.0) in neurons overexpressing NLG1 compared to paired non-electroporated controls, reflecting the well-known synaptogenic effect of NLG1 (Kwon et al., 2012; Shipman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data from organotypic slices and citations to previous studies (Kwon et al., 2012; Shipman et al., 2011).

claim: NLG1 overexpression was associated with a decrease in the coefficient of variation (CV).
source: This effect was associated with a decrease in the coefficient of variation (CV) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neurons expressing NLG1-ΔCter exhibited a limited ~2 fold increase in AMPAR-mediated EPSC amplitude (226.0 ± 59.1) compared to control neurons.
source: In contrast, neurons expressing NLG1-ΔCter exhibited a limited ~2 fold increase in AMPAR-mediated EPSC amplitude (226.0 ± 59.1) and no change in CV compared to control neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neurons expressing NLG1-ΔCter showed no change in CV compared to control neurons.
source: In contrast, neurons expressing NLG1-ΔCter exhibited a limited ~2 fold increase in AMPAR-mediated EPSC amplitude (226.0 ± 59.1) and no change in CV compared to control neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant change in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) upon expression of either NLG1 or NLG1-ΔCter.
source: Finally, there was no significant change in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) upon expression of either NLG1 or NLG1-ΔCter (Figure 4—figure supplement 4; PPR for NLG1: control 1.63 ± 0.11, NLG1 1.36 ± 0.09, for NLG1-ΔCter), indicating no specific modification of the pre-synaptic release probability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both NLG1 and NLG1-ΔCter expression increased the frequency of asynchronous EPSCs compared to non-electroporated neurons.
source: Both NLG1 and NLG1-ΔCter expression increased the frequency of asynchronous EPSCs compared to non-electroporated neurons, again reflecting the synaptogenic effect of NLG1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The amplitude of asynchronous EPSCs was reduced by 26% in neurons expressing NLG1-ΔCter but not in neurons expressing NLG1, when compared to control non-electroporated neurons.
source: Moreover, as observed with miniatures in dissociated cultures, the amplitude of asynchronous EPSCs was reduced by 26% in neurons expressing NLG1-ΔCter but not in neurons expressing NLG1, when compared to control non-electroporated neurons (Figure 4H and I, for NLG1 expression: control: 11.59 ± 0.73, NLG1: 11.60 ± 1.03; for NLG1-ΔCter expression: control: 12.01 ± 1.56, NLG1-ΔCter: 8.893 ± 0.70; paired t-test p=0.99 and 0.018).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4H and I with statistical analysis (paired t-test p=0.99 and 0.018).

claim: A 32% decrease of asynchronous EPSC amplitude was observed on NLG1-ΔCter expressing neurons relatively to unelectroporated counterparts in the NLG1 KO background.
source: Similar results were obtained on the NLG1 KO background (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), with a 32% decrease of asynchronous EPSC amplitude on NLG1-ΔCter expressing neurons relatively to unelectroporated counterparts.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: NLG1-ΔCter directly affects the quantal size.
source: Together, these results show that NLG1-ΔCter directly affects the quantal size, which is compatible with our concept of synaptic mis-alignment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental electrophysiology data on asynchronous EPSCs presented in the preceding sentences.

claim: Incubation of hippocampal neurons with NLG1 competing ligands decreased the co-localization between RIM and GluA2 containing AMPARs.
source: Incubation of 14 DIV hippocampal neurons for 1–2 days with NLG1 competing ligands decreased the co-localization between RIM and GluA2 containing AMPARs observed by dual-color d-STORM (Figure 5A–C), and reduced by 30% AMPAR-mediated mEPSC amplitudes (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental d-STORM data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Incubation of hippocampal neurons with NLG1 competing ligands reduced by 30% AMPAR-mediated mEPSC amplitudes.
source: Incubation of 14 DIV hippocampal neurons for 1–2 days with NLG1 competing ligands decreased the co-localization between RIM and GluA2 containing AMPARs observed by dual-color d-STORM (Figure 5A–C), and reduced by 30% AMPAR-mediated mEPSC amplitudes (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Control non-sense TAT peptides had no effect on RIM-AMPAR co-localization compared to untreated neurons.
source: In both assays, control non-sense TAT peptides had no effect compared to untreated neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: NLG1 peptides did not alter AMPAR-mediated mEPSC frequency.
source: Interestingly, NLG1 peptides did not alter AMPAR-mediated mEPSC frequency (Figure 5F), suggesting an exclusive post-synaptic effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: NLG1 competing peptides and NLG1-ΔCter expression had very similar effects on AMPAR positioning and synaptic responses.
source: Overall, NLG1 competing peptides and NLG1-ΔCter expression had very similar effects on AMPAR positioning and synaptic responses, suggesting a common mechanism of action.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparison of experimental results with NLG1 peptides and NLG1-ΔCter expression.

claim: The number of released glutamate molecules was fixed to 1500, 2000, 3000 or 4500 in the simulations, to be in the range of the estimated amount per pre-synaptic vesicle.
source: In the simulations, the number of released glutamate molecules was fixed to 1500, 2000, 3000 or 4500, to be in the range of the estimated amount per pre-synaptic vesicle (Savtchenko et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study estimating glutamate content per vesicle (Savtchenko et al., 2013).

claim: The glutamate content per pre-synaptic vesicle was positively correlated with the synaptic response in simulations.
source: As expected, simulated curves demonstrated that the glutamate content per pre-synaptic vesicle was positively correlated with the synaptic response (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The number of opened AMPAR was inversely correlated to the distance between the release site and AMPAR nanodomains in simulations.
source: Strikingly, the simulation further showed that the number of opened AMPAR was inversely correlated to the distance between the release site and AMPAR nanodomains (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A release of 3000 glutamate molecules at 150 nm from an AMPAR nanodomain led to a decrease of almost 40% of the synaptic response in simulations.
source: A release of 3000 glutamate molecules, which is in the upper range of glutamate content per vesicle, at 150 nm from an AMPAR nanodomain, led to a decrease of almost 40% of the synaptic response.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results described in the text.

claim: The glutamate diffusion coefficient drastically changed the synaptic transmission efficiency without altering the tight correlation between synaptic transmission and pre-post alignment.
source: The first parameter drastically changed the synaptic transmission efficiency (i.e. the lower the glutamate diffusion coefficient, the higher AMPA currents) without altering the tight correlation between synaptic transmission and pre-post alignment.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results described in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: AMPAR-mediated currents are independent with respect to the astrocyte-dependent clearance of the glutamate released from a single vesicle.
source: The second parameter revealed the independence of AMPAR-mediated currents with respect to the astrocyte-dependent clearance of the glutamate released from a single vesicle.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results described in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: NLG1 plays an important role in the organization of trans-synaptic 'nano-columns', by positioning AMPAR nanodomains in close proximity to pre-synaptic release sites.
source: First, NLG1 seems to play an important role in the organization of trans-synaptic 'nano-columns', by positioning AMPAR nanodomains in close proximity to pre-synaptic release sites.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The amplitude of AMPAR-mediated currents is highly sensitive to pre-post synaptic nanoscale alignment.
source: Second, the amplitude of AMPAR-mediated currents is highly sensitive to pre-post synaptic nanoscale alignment (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and computational modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: NLG1 binds pre-synaptic neurexins via its extracellular domain.
source: NLG1 binds pre-synaptic neurexins via its extracellular domain, while its cytoplasmic tail exhibits various binding sites including a C-terminal PDZ domain binding motif, a central gephyrin binding motif, and an upstream non-canonical motif without identified interactor but also important for neuroligin function (Dean et al., 2003; Giannone et al., 2013; Irie et al., 1997; Shipman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Dean et al., 2003; Giannone et al., 2013; Irie et al., 1997; Shipman et al., 2011).

claim: NLG1's cytoplasmic tail exhibits a C-terminal PDZ domain binding motif.
source: NLG1 binds pre-synaptic neurexins via its extracellular domain, while its cytoplasmic tail exhibits various binding sites including a C-terminal PDZ domain binding motif, a central gephyrin binding motif, and an upstream non-canonical motif without identified interactor but also important for neuroligin function (Dean et al., 2003; Giannone et al., 2013; Irie et al., 1997; Shipman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Dean et al., 2003; Giannone et al., 2013; Irie et al., 1997; Shipman et al., 2011).

claim: NLG1's cytoplasmic tail exhibits a central gephyrin binding motif.
source: NLG1 binds pre-synaptic neurexins via its extracellular domain, while its cytoplasmic tail exhibits various binding sites including a C-terminal PDZ domain binding motif, a central gephyrin binding motif, and an upstream non-canonical motif without identified interactor but also important for neuroligin function (Dean et al., 2003; Giannone et al., 2013; Irie et al., 1997; Shipman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Dean et al., 2003; Giannone et al., 2013; Irie et al., 1997; Shipman et al., 2011).

claim: When expressed during the early stages of synaptogenesis, NLG1-ΔCter is able to strongly increase synapse number, but does not recruit enough PSD-95 and AMPARs to sustain normal synaptic transmission.
source: When expressed during the early stages of synaptogenesis, this NLG1 mutant is able to strongly increase synapse number, but does not recruit enough PSD-95 and AMPARs to sustain normal synaptic transmission (Budreck et al., 2013; Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Budreck et al., 2013; Mondin et al., 2011; Nam and Chen, 2005).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter outcompeted the endogenous NLG1 for the binding to neurexins, allowing unanchored PSD-95 scaffolds and connected AMPAR nanodomains to flow away from the release site.
source: Our interpretation is that NLG1-ΔCter outcompeted the endogenous NLG1 for the binding to neurexins (or/and other pre-synaptic partners), allowing unanchored PSD-95 scaffolds and connected AMPAR nanodomains to flow away from the release site (MacGillavry et al., 2013; Nair et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of their experimental results, with citations to previous studies (MacGillavry et al., 2013; Nair et al., 2013).

claim: Heterodimerization might occur between recombinant NLG1-ΔCter and endogenous NLG1.
source: As previously published, heterodimerization might occur between recombinant NLG1-ΔCter and endogenous NLG1 (Shipman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Shipman et al., 2011).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter might heterodimerize with NLG3.
source: Interestingly, a similar reduction in AMPAR currents induced by NLG1-ΔCter was observed in organotypic slices from both NLG1 WT and KO genetic backgrounds, revealing a potential heterodimerization of NLG1-ΔCter with other NLGs, most likely NLG3 (Shipman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results in NLG1 KO background, with a citation to a previous study (Shipman et al., 2011).

claim: C-terminal interactions between NLG1 and PDZ domain containing scaffolding proteins such as PSD-95 are important to align AMPAR nanodomains in front of pre-synaptic release sites.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that C-terminal interactions between NLG1 and PDZ domain containing scaffolding proteins such as PSD-95, are important to align AMPAR nanodomains in front of pre-synaptic release sites.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with NLG1-ΔCter and NLG1 peptides presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A displacement of AMPAR nanodomain of less than 100 nm decreases mEPSC amplitude by about 30%.
source: The functional effect of such a molecular disorganization caused either by NLG1-ΔCter expression or NLG1 peptide incubation was found to be unexpectedly important, that is a displacement of AMPAR nanodomain of less than 100 nm decreases mEPSC amplitude by about 30%.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental electrophysiology and imaging results presented in the manuscript.

claim: An equivalent 25% decrease of current could be explained by either a 3-fold decrease in glutamate content (from 4500 to 1500 molecules per vesicle), a 32% loss in the number of AMPARs per nanodomain, or a 100 nm shift between pre- and post-organization (for a glutamate content of 2000 molecules per vesicle).
source: Our simulations predict that an equivalent 25% decrease of current could be explained by either a 3-fold decrease in glutamate content (from 4500 to 1500 molecules per vesicle), a 32% loss in the number of AMPARs per nanodomain, or a 100 nm shift between pre- and post-organization (for a glutamate content of 2000 molecules per vesicle), underlying the high sensitivity of synaptic currents to pre-post alignment.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results described in the text.

claim: Action potential-dependent currents recorded from slices in calcium or strontium conditions combine the synaptogenic effect of NLG1 via its extracellular interaction with pre-synaptic adhesion proteins (affecting parameter n) and its role in AMPAR recruitment and pre-post alignment (affecting parameter q).
source: Action potential-dependent currents recorded from slices in calcium or strontium conditions do not directly reflect the synaptic response because they combine (i) the synaptogenic effect of NLG1 via its extracellular interaction with pre-synaptic adhesion proteins, which affect the parameter n and (ii) its role in AMPAR recruitment and pre-post alignment, affecting the parameter q.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and established knowledge about synaptic transmission parameters.

claim: The absence of effect on the paired pulse properties indicates that the p value should not be affected by NLG1 and NLG1-ΔCter expression.
source: First, the absence of effect on the paired pulse properties (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) indicates that the p value should not be affected by NLG1 and NLG1-ΔCter expression.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental paired-pulse data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and established knowledge about paired-pulse ratio.

claim: The net increase of EPSC amplitude in calcium conditions induced by both NLG1 and NLG1-ΔCter compared to control neurons can be attributed to an increase of the n parameter by recruiting additional pre-synapses.
source: Second, the net increase of EPSC amplitude in calcium conditions induced by both NLG1 and NLG1-ΔCter compared to control neurons can be attributed to an increase of the n parameter by recruiting additional pre-synapses, as abundantly described in the literature and shown Figure 1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and citations to literature.

claim: The significant decrease of evoked AMPAR-mediated EPSC amplitude caused by NLG1-ΔCter with respect to NLG1, combined with the increase in CV, can be attributed to either a recruitment of silent synapses by NLG1-ΔCter, or a decrease of the quantal size (q) due to pre-post synaptic mis-alignment.
source: However, the significant decrease of evoked AMPAR-mediated EPSC amplitude caused by NLG1-ΔCter with respect to NLG1, combined with the increase in CV is more difficult to explain. It can be attributed to either a recruitment of silent synapses by NLG1-ΔCter, or a decrease of the quantal size (q) due for example to pre-post synaptic mis-alignment.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about possible explanations for the experimental observations.

claim: Spontaneous miniature currents recorded in calcium and asynchronous EPSCs recorded in strontium suggest that NLG1-ΔCter expression affects both action potential-dependent and -independent synaptic transmission.
source: However, taken together, spontaneous miniature currents recorded in calcium and asynchronous EPSCs recorded in strontium suggest that NLG1-ΔCter expression affects both action potential-dependent and -independent synaptic transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental electrophysiology results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synapses exhibit a relative tolerance to variability both in the glutamate content per vesicle and in the number of AMPAR per nanodomain.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: A 10–20% variation in glutamate content per vesicle and number of AMPAR per nanodomain will not drastically affect synaptic transmission efficacy.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fast and large modifications in synaptic amplitude can be better achieved by molecular pre-post misalignment than by changes in AMPAR number.
source: Second, fast and large modifications in synaptic amplitude can be better achieved by molecular pre-post misalignment than by changes in AMPAR number.

claim: The amplitude of AMPAR currents is not sensitive to the glutamate clearance by glial cells.
source: Interestingly, our modeling data predict that the amplitude of AMPAR currents is not sensitive to the glutamate clearance by glial cells, in agreement with the model that AMPAR activation takes place within the 100 nm surrounding the release site.

claim: High efficiency of synaptic transmission, high amplitude response and low variability, requires a tight clustering of AMPA receptors, and an alignment of these clusters with the pre-synaptic release site.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous modeling studies (Nair et al., 2013; Tarusawa et al., 2009).

claim: Synapses optimize the use of glutamate by controlling the alignment between pre-synaptic release sites and AMPAR nanodomains via NLG1-based trans-synaptic adhesion, with surprisingly high sensitivity.
source: Our study proposes that synapses, via NLG1-based trans-synaptic adhesion, optimize the use of glutamate by controlling the alignment between pre-synaptic release sites and AMPAR nanodomains, with surprisingly high sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from all the experimental and computational results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of NLG1-ΔCter suppresses the co-localization of NLG1 and AMPAR nanodomains without changing the overall AMPAR nanoscale organization.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental d-STORM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AMPARs mediate the vast majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the mammalian brain.
source: AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) mediate the vast majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the mammalian brain.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about AMPAR function.

claim: AMPARs are stabilized at the post-synaptic density (PSD) by interactions with PDZ domain containing proteins such as PSD-95.
source: AMPARs are stabilized at the post-synaptic density (PSD) by interactions with PDZ domain containing proteins such as PSD-95.

source: Nanodomains are determined as clusters of AMPARs present inside the synapse and containing at least 5 receptors, based on single particle emission properties (see Nair et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the methodological definition used in the study, based on a citation to Nair et al., 2013.

claim: AMPAR nanodomains are tightly associated with PSD-95 sites.
source: Given that AMPAR nanodomains are tightly associated with PSD-95 sites (MacGillavry et al., 2013; Nair et al., 2013), our rationale was that by disconnecting NLG1 from PSD-95, we would perturb the nanoscale positioning of AMPARs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (MacGillavry et al., 2013; Nair et al., 2013).

claim: NLG1-ΔCter has an intact extracellular domain allowing normal contacts with pre-synaptic partners such as neurexins.
source: NLG1-ΔCter has an intact extracellular domain allowing normal contacts with pre-synaptic partners such as neurexins (Chih et al., 2005; Mondin et al., 2011), but is unable to interact with cytoplasmic proteins within the PSD, and thus should behave as a dominant-negative mutant that uncouples trans-synaptic adhesion from the PSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chih et al., 2005; Mondin et al., 2011).
